# Applied Heat Written Examination Syllabus

Published 6 May 2014

## Contents

1. 1\. Pressure, temperature and energy
2. 2\. Heat transfer
3. 3\. Internal energy, thermo-dynamic systems, first law
4. 4\. Gas laws, displacement work
5. 5\. Ideal Cycles and I.C. engines
6. 6\. Air compressors
7. 7\. Working fluids
8. 8\. Nozzles and steam turbines
9. 9\. Refrigeration
10. 10\. Combustion
11. 11\. Boiler feed densities

Print this page

This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit [nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3) or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: [psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk](mailto:psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk) .

Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned.

This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/second-engineer-written-examination-syllabuses/applied-heat-written-examination-syllabus

## 1\. Pressure, temperature and energy

### 1\.1 Recognises and measures the effect of pressure in fluid

1. Defines pressure as force per unit area.
2. Recognises the effect of atmospheric pressure.
3. States that standard atmospheric pressure is 1.01325 bar = 1.01325 x 10 ⁵ N/m ² .
4. Measures atmospheric pressure using a mercury barometer.
5. Converts pressure units using water lead, mercury lead with bar units.
6. Defines:
   
    1. vacuum;
    2. partial vacuum;
    3. gauge pressure;
    4. absolute pressure.
7. Solves simple problems relating to 1.1.1 to 1.1.6.

### 1\.2 Defines and measures temperature

1. Defines temperature.
2. Defines the absolute scale of temperature.
3. Differentiates between Celsius and Kelvin Scales.
4. Defines Standard Temperature and Pressure (S.T.P.) and Normal Temperature and Pressure (N.P.T.).

### 1\.3 Discusses heat as a form of energy, specific heat capacity, sensible heat, latent heat and solves associated problems.

1. Defines heat energy.
2. Defines specific heat capacity of a solid and of a liquid.
3. Defines sensible heat.
4. Explains phase change and defines the latent heat of fusion.
5. Sketches the change of phase (solid/liquid) diagram for water.
6. Determines the resultant temperature when a solid is placed in a liquid at a different temperature.
7. Determines the resultant temperature when up to three liquids at different temperatures are mixed.
8. Defines water equivalent.
9. Solves simple problems relating to 1.3.1 to 1.3.8.

### 1\.4 Discusses the physical changes of solids and liquids associated with changes in temperature

1. Defines the coefficient of linear expansion.
2. States the equation of linear expansion/contraction.
3. States the equation of superficial expansion.
4. States that the coefficient of volumetric expansion is three times the coefficient of linear expansion.
5. States the equation of volumetric expansion.
6. Defines differential expansion with reference to solids and liquids.
7. Solves simple problems relating to 1.4.1 to 1.4.6.

## 2\. Heat transfer

### 2\.1 Describes the way in which heat may be transferred and the factors which may influence heat transfer. Solves simple problems involving conduction, convection and radiation.

1. Describes heat transfer by conduction.
2. Gives practical examples of heat transfer by conduction.
3. Defines the term coefficient of thermal conductivity.
4. States an expression for the rate of heat transfer through a single plane wall.
5. States that for a composite wall the rate of heat transfer is constant.
6. States an expression for the transfer of heat through a composite wall made up of not more than three flat layers in contact.
7. Solves simple problems relating to 2.1.1 to 2.1.6.
8. Describes heat transfer by convection.
9. Lists practical examples of forced and natural convection.
10. Defines the term ‘coefficient of conductance’.
11. States an expression for the rate of heat transfer from a flat surface to its surroundings.
12. Solves simple problems relating to 2.1.8 to 2.1.11.
13. Describes heat transfer by radiation.
14. Gives practical examples of heat transfer by radiation.

## 3\. Internal energy, thermo-dynamic systems, first law

### 3\.1 Defines and describes Thermo-dynamic Systems and solves problems involving the First Law of Thermodynamics

1. Defines Internal Energy.
2. States Joules Law for the internal energy of a gas.
3. Defines a Thermodynamic system.
4. Differentiates between an open and a closed system.
5. Give examples of:
   
    1. closed system with fixed boundary (constant volume);
    2. closed system with elastic boundary (constant pressure);
    3. open system with fixed boundary.
6. Defines work with reference to a thermodynamic system.
7. States the First Law of Thermodynamics in terms of heat energy, work energy and internal energy.
8. States that Q = W + U and that this is the non-flow energy equation.
9. States that power is the rate of transfer of energy.
10. States that H + Q = H + W and that this is the flow energy equation.
11. Solves simple problems relating to 3.1.1 to 3.1.10.

## 4\. Gas laws, displacement work

### 4\.1 Solves simple problems involving the basic gas laws

1. Defines a perfect gas.
2. States Boyles Law.
3. States Charles Law.
4. Shows Boyles Law and Charles Law on a pV diagram.
5. Combines Boyles Law and Charles Law and states that for a perfect gas pV/T = a constant.
6. Derives the Characteristic Gas Equation pV = mRT.
7. Derives the units of the Characteristic Gas Constant R from the units of pressure, volume, temperature and mass.
8. Solves simple problems relating to 4.1.1 to 4.1.7.

### 4\.2 Describes processes which will produce a change of state in a non-flow system and solves problems concerned with non-flow processes

1. Differentiates between constant pressure and constant volume operations.
2. Defines specific heat capacities of a gas at constant pressure and at constant volume.
3. States that the ratio of the specific heat capacities of a gas Cp/Cv = γ (gamma) the adiabatic index.
4. Defines:
   
    1. an Isothermal operation;
    2. an Adiabatic operation;
    3. a Polytropic operation.
5. Shows the Isothermal, Adiabatic and Polytropic Operations on a pV diagram
6. Shows that the area of the pV diagram represents W.D. during the operation.
7. States expressions for the work done during isothermal, adiabatic and polytropic non-flow processes. T ₂ /T ₁ = P ₂ /P ₁ = V ₁ /V ₂
8. States the temperature - pressure and temperature -volume relations for an operation to the law pV = a constant.
9. States that change in internal energy is given by mC v (T ₂ \- T ₁ )
10. States that the relationship between the Characteristic Gas Constant and the specific heat capacities of a gas is R = (C ρ \- C v ).
11. Solves simple problems relating to 4.2.1 to 4.2.10.

## 5\. Ideal Cycles and I.C. engines

### 5\.1 Sketches p - V diagram and describes the operation for the ideal constant volume (Otto) cycle, the Diesel cycle and the Dual Combustion cycle

1. Sketches the pV diagram for the ideal Otto, Diesel and Dual Combustion cycles and names the processes making up these cycles.
2. Names the practical engines that operate on these cycles.
3. Compares the ideal cycle with the practical four stroke cycle.
4. Gives reasons for the differences between the ideal and the practical cycle.
5. Answers simple descriptive questions only on the Otto, Diesel and Dual Combustion cycles.
6. Defines air standard efficiency and solves problems involving engine cycles.

### 5\.2 Determines indicated power, brake power and mechanical efficiency of an I.C. engine and solves problems involving power, efficiency, fuel consumption and heat balance

1. Defines mean effective pressure (m.e.p.).
2. Determines the area of an indicator card using the mid-ordinate rule.
3. States the terms, spring rate, spring stiffness and spring constant when referred to indicators.
4. Determines the indicated m.e.p. from an actual indicator diagram.
5. Defines indicated power.
6. Derives an expression for calculating indicated power.
7. Defines brake power.
8. Defines brake mean effective pressure (b.m.e.p.) and uses this term in the determination of brake power.
9. Derives an expression for brake power in terms of torque and angular velocity.
10. Determines mechanical efficiency.
11. Calculates indicated power, brake power and mechanical efficiency from engine test data.
12. Defines thermal efficiency for an actual engine.
13. Differentiates between brake and indicated thermal efficiencies.
14. Calculates thermal efficiency from engine data.
15. Defines specific fuel consumption based on indicated power and brake power.
16. Relates specific fuel consumption to thermal efficiency.
17. Calculates specific fuel consumption from engine data.
18. Draws up a heat energy balance for an I.C. engine.
19. Solves simple problems relating to 5.2.1 to 5.2.18.
20. Solves problems involving thermal, mechanical and overall efficiency.

## 6\. Air compressors

### 6\.1 Describes the factors which influence the performance of a reciprocating air compressor and solves simple problems involving single stage single acting compressors.

1. Sketches the ideal p - V diagram for a compressor without clearance volume.
2. Sketches the ideal p - V diagram for a compressor with clearance volume.
3. Defines clearance volume.
4. Defines induced volume.
5. Defines ‘free air’ delivery for an air compressor.
6. Defines volumetric efficiency based on ‘free air’ and actual air conditions. V = ActualVolumeInduced/ SweptVolume
7. Solves simple problems relating to 6.1.1 to 6.1.6.
8. Solves problems involving work input and mechanic efficiency.

## 7\.  Working fluids

### 7\.1 Recognises the differences in the properties of vapours, gases and the perfect gas and uses the steam tables to solve simple problems related to water and steam in the wet, saturated and superheated states

1. Differentiate between a gas and a perfect gas.
2. Differentiate between a gas and a vapour.
3. Defines the term ENTHALPY (h).
4. States that h = u + pV.
5. Defines the term pV as flow energy.
6. Shows that pV is the work transfer in pumping a fluid under constant pressure conditions.
7. Defines the term ‘saturated’ when applied to a vapour.
8. Defines saturation temperature.
9. Differentiates between wet, dry-saturated and superheated vapours.
10. Defines the term dryness fraction.
11. Defines the terms ‘quality’ and ‘degree of superheat’ as applied to a vapour.
12. Demonstrates how to obtain values of specific enthalpy, specific volume and internal energy for water and for wet dry saturated and superheated vapours from the Thermodynamic Properties tables by direct reading or interpolation.
13. Sketches a pressure-enthalpy diagram.
14. States that the specific enthalpy of a wet vapour is given by hf + x hfg.
15. States that the specific internal energy of a wet vapour is given by uf + x ufg.
16. States that the specific volume of wet vapour is given by x Vg + (1 - x) Vf.
17. Determines from information given in the tables the pressure- temperature relationship for a saturated vapour.
18. Determines the mass of a given volume of wet, dry or superheated vapour.
19. Calculates changes in the enthalpy and internal energy of a vapour during constant pressure and constant volume operation.
20. States that an operation following the law pV n = a constant is a hyperbolic operation when the working fluid is a vapour.
21. Calculates the final condition of the vapour after an operation to the law pV n = a constant.
22. States that for a throttling operation on a vapour enthalpy before throttling = enthalpy after throttling.
23. Solves problem relating to 7.1.1 to 7.1.22.
24. Sketches the arrangement of a combined separator and throttling calorimeter.
25. Determines the quality of steam in a main line from data obtained using the combined separator and throttling calorimeter.
26. States the limitations of pressure and dryness fraction which apply to the throttling calorimeter.
27. Determines Boiler Efficiency and Equivalent Evaporation rates from given plant data.
28. Solves simple problems relating to 7.1.1 to 7.1.27.

## 8\. Nozzles and steam turbines

### 8\.1 Solves simple problems involving the flow of steam through a nozzle.

1. Defines a nozzle and gives practical applications of where nozzles are used in a steam turbine.
2. Recognises that increase in K.E. at nozzle exit is proportional to the enthalpy drop.
3. Solves simple problems relating to 8.1.1 to 8.1.2.
4. Sketches the combined velocity diagrams and determines the power developed in a single stage impulse turbine and a single stage reaction turbine.
5. Draws the vector diagrams for inlet and outlet steam velocities over a turbine blade for shockless flow.
6. Combines the inlet and outlet diagrams to form a single diagram.
7. Shows velocity of whirl on a combined diagram.
8. Shows the effect of blade friction (blade velocity coefficient).
9. States an expression for the power developed in a single stage of an impulse turbine.
10. Solves problems relating to 8.1.1 to 8.1.5.
11. Draws the combined velocity diagram for a single stage reaction turbine.
12. Discusses degree of reaction and states that 50% reaction is usual and refers to a Parsons turbine.
13. States an expression for the power developed in a reaction turbine pair.
14. Solves simple problems relating to 8.1.12 to 8.1.13.
15. Solves problems involving axial force on blades.

## 9\. Refrigeration

### 9\.1 Understands the concepts of the reversed heat engine cycle and its applications to vapour compression refrigeration plant and solves simple problems

1. Sketches the circuit diagram for the basic vapour compression refrigeration cycle.
2. Identifies the principal components of a vapour compression refrigerator and describes its operation.
3. Sketches a vapour compression cycle on a p - h diagram showing:
   
    1. wetness before entering compressor;
    2. dryness before entering compressor;
    3. superheat before entering compressor;
    4. superheat after entering compressor;
    5. undercooling after condenser.
4. Defines ‘refrigerating effect’ in kJ/kg, mass flow rate in kg/s and ‘cooling load’ in kW.
5. Shows that work transfer from the compressor during an adiabatic operation is equal to the enthalpy change of the vapour.
6. Defines ‘coefficient of performance’ of a refrigeration plant.
7. Defines ‘capacity’ of a refrigeration plant.
8. Uses property tables to determine the specific enthalpy and specific volume of wet, dry and superheated refrigerants.
9. Solves simple problems relating to 9.1.1 to 9.1.8.

## 10\. Combustion

### 10\.1 Discusses the combustion of solid and liquid fuels by mass in terms of theoretical air and excess air required and the products of combustion. Solves problems involving the combustion of a fuel

1. Defines the chemical definitions of atom, molecule, atomic mass, molecular mass, element, compound and a mixture.
2. States the combustion equations for the complete combustion of Carbon to Carbon Dioxide, Hydrogen to Water, and Sulphur to Sulphur Dioxide.
3. States the equation for the partial combustion of Carbon to Carbon Monoxide.
4. Derives the equations for the combustion of simple hydro-carbon fuels.
5. States that air contains approximately 23% oxygen and 77% nitrogen by mass.
6. Determines the stoichimetric mass of air required for the complete combustion of a hydro-carbon fuel.
7. Determines the percentage excess air required for complete combustion of a hydro-carbon fuel.
8. Defines the Higher Calorific Value and the Lower Calorific Value of a fuel.
9. Determines the Higher and Lower Calorific Values of a fuel given the calorific value of its constituents.
10. Lists on a percentage basis the products of combustion of a fuel, burned in excess air, by mass.
11. Solves problems relating to 10.1.1 to 10.1.10.

## 11\. Boiler feed densities

### 11\.1 Discusses the effects of using feed water containing dissolved solids on boiler and evaporator plant. Solves simple problems on the change in density of boiler and evaporator plant due to build up of dissolved solids during intermittent and continuous blowdown

1. Defines parts per million (ppm).
2. Discusses the meaning of density when referring to dissolved solids in boiler or evaporator feed water.
3. Determines the change in density of the boiler or evaporator water content when operating with:
   
    1. no blowdown;
    2. intermittent blowdown;
    3. continuous blowdown.
4. Determines the heat lost to blowdown.
5. Defines boiler efficiency.
6. Solves simple problems relating to 11.1.1 to 11.1.5.

# Marine Electro-Technology Written Examination Syllabus

Published 6 May 2014

## Contents

1. 1\. Electric and electronic components
2. 2\. Electric circuit principles
3. 3\. Electromagnetism
4. 4\. Electrical machines

Print this page

This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit [nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3](https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3) or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: [psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk](mailto:psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk) .

Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned.

This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/second-engineer-written-examination-syllabuses/marine-electro-technology-written-examination-syllabus

## 1\. Electric and electronic components

### 1\.1 Understands the physical construction and characteristics of basic components

1. Compares the characteristics of conductors, semi-conductors and insulators in terms of the Electron Theory.
2. Defines the basic quantities of electricity, eg charge, current, emf, potential difference, energy and power.
3. Describes resistance, inductance and capacitance in terms of physical dimensions and materials.
4. Solves numerical problems relating R, L and C to their physical parameters.
5. Appreciates how temperature affects conductors, semi-conductors and insulators.
6. Defines temperature coefficient of resistance at 0°C (α ο ) and also at a stated temperature (α t ).
7. Calculates change in conductor resistance using the temperature coefficients in 1.1.6.
8. Draws and labels the principal parts of a lead acid cell.
9. Describes (without using chemical formulae) the action of charge and discharge on the components of the cell.
10. Explains how the state of charge of a lead acid cell may be measured using a hydrometer.
11. Draws and labels the principal parts of an alkaline cell, Nickel iron or nickel cadmium.
12. Explains how the state of charge may be assessed for alkaline cells.
13. Compares lead acid and alkaline cells on the basis of:
    
    1. voltage per cell;
    2. performance under poor conditions of charge/discharge;
    3. retention of charge;
    4. effect of temperature;
    5. mechanical strength;
    6. weight;
    7. cost.
14. States that the capacity of a battery is measured in ampere hours at a given rate.
15. Solves problems on efficiency of batteries in terms of ampere-hours and watt-hours.
16. Solves problems involving batteries in series and in parallel combinations including internal resistance and current in a connected load.
17. Draws a simple charging circuit from a dc supply.
18. Measures the state of charge of a battery before and after carrying out the charging procedure.
19. States the two common types of semi conductor material as germanium and silicon.
20. Explains the formation of ‘p’ type and ‘n’ type semi conductor materials referring to the doping process.
21. Draws a p-n junction in forward and reverse bias modes and indicates electron flow and conventional current flow in the junction and in the external circuit.
22. Obtains the static characteristic curves for forward and reverse biasing of the pn junction from test results.
23. States the need for rectification of alternating voltages.
24. Explains and draws circuit diagrams to show how rectification of an ac single phase supply is obtained using:
    
    1. one diode;
    2. two diodes and centre tapped transformer; and
    3. bridge connected diodes.
25. Draws the input and output waveforms for the rectifier circuits in 1.1.24.
26. Explains the formation of a pnp and npn alloy junction transistor.
27. Draws a circuit diagram showing pnp and npn transistors connected in the common emitter mode.
28. Draws and explains a circuit diagram illustrating the use of a transistor as a switch.
29. Draws and explains a circuit diagram illustrating the use of a transistor as an alternating small signal amplifier.
30. Describes the photo-electric effect and its application to photo-diodes.
31. State some marine applications of 1.1.28 and 1.1.30.

## 2\. Electric circuit principles

### 2\.1 Understands the operation of simple linear dc and ac electrical circuits and solves related problems

1. States Ohms Law.
2. Solves problems on 2.1.1.
3. States Kirchhoffs Current Law.
4. States Kirchhoffs Voltage Law.
5. Describes a series circuit configuration using a variety of components and finds the equivalent resistance.
6. Describes a parallel circuit configuration using a variety of components and finds the equivalent resistance.
7. Solves problems on series/parallel circuits.
8. Solves problems on power and energy in dc resistive circuits.
9. Solves problems using Kirchhoffs laws by application of simultaneous equations (two unknowns only).
10. Explains the principle of the Wheatstone bridge and derives the balance equation.
11. Solves problems related to 2.1.10.
12. Defines an alternating emf in terms of its maximum value, rms level, periodic time, frequency and its time equation.
13. States that e = E MAX sin 2reft volts.
14. Explains that the resultant current will also be sinusoidal and represented by i = I MAX sin 21-rft amperes.
15. Solves problems related to 2.1.13 and 2.1.14.
16. Draws the wave forms for above and indicates peak value; peak to peak value; periodic time; frequency.
17. Explains terms, mean value, rms value and form factor with reference to a sine wave.
18. Calculates the rms value, mean value and form factor of sinusoidal and non-sinusoidal wave forms.
19. Explains the term phasor quantity.
20. Explains how phasors may be used to represent sinusoidal quantities.
21. Solves graphical problems involving addition and subtraction of ac voltages and currents using phasor method.
22. Sketches the current, voltage and power waveform patterns of a pure:
    
    1. resistor;
    2. inductor;
    3. capacitor;
